query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In selective laser melting (SLM) of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), implementing an optimized substrate preheating step will reduce thermal gradients during processing, thereby lowering the build’s residual stresses and defect formation. Consequently, the fabricated component will exhibit enhanced dimensional precision and mechanical integrity with reduced porosity and cracking relative to parts built without preheating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built HEA components (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn) produced via SLM that typically have rapid solidification‐induced defects such as internal pores, high dislocation densities, and residual stress–driven geometric distortions.
generation.intervention: Introduce substrate preheating at a controlled, optimized temperature (e.g., in the range of 200–400°C) during the SLM process.
generation.conditions: Processing under standard SLM parameters (laser power, scanning speed, powder characteristics) for HEAs, with the only variable being the application of substrate preheating; applicable to components with complex geometries where dimensional accuracy and integrity are critical.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients between the melt pool and the substrate lead to lower residual stress accumulation and a more uniform solidification process, which in turn decreases the formation of porosity, cracks, and other defects.
generation.mechanism: Substrate preheating raises the base temperature of the build, thereby narrowing the temperature differential during melting and solidification. This moderation in thermal shock diminishes rapid cooling-induced defects, limits internal stress development, and promotes a more homogeneous microstructure that enhances both dimensional fidelity and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (non-preheated SLM builds), samples fabricated with preheated substrates will show improved dimensional accuracy, lower defect densities (e.g., fewer pores and cracks), and enhanced mechanical properties such as higher yield strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: HEA components built using conventional SLM processes without substrate preheating, which typically exhibit higher residual stresses, more fabrication-induced defects, and dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under conventional SLM conditions for HEAs; however, the optimal preheating temperature window may vary between alloy systems and could be less effective if the temperature is not properly tuned. Extreme process conditions or different AM techniques might not yield the same improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal preheating temperature and its quantitative impact on mechanical properties require further empirical determination. The magnitude of defect reduction and property enhancement may also depend on specific alloy compositions and SLM parameters not fully captured by current evidence.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA components using SLM: one set with the substrate maintained at room temperature (baseline) and the other set with substrate preheating at designated temperatures (e.g., 200°C, 300°C, 400°C). All other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, powder characteristics) are kept identical.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy using 3D scanning or coordinate measuring machines.
Microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM for porosity, EBSD for grain structure and defect density).
Mechanical testing (tensile tests for yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility).
Residual stress analysis via X-ray diffraction (XRD) or other suitable methods.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, reduced defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study uniquely demonstrates the processability, hot-cracking susceptibility, and in situ mechanical response of CoCrFeNiCu-HEA fabricated by L-PBF, providing new insights into defect evolution and mechanical performance under these specific processing conditions. Future work will focus on targeted alloying (e.g., Al addition), pre-heating strategies, and optimized scanning to further reduce hot-cracking susceptibility and enhance mechanical performance. This study provides insights into the processability, defect evolution, and mechanical response of L-PBF CoCrFeNiCu-HEA, guiding the development of crack-resistant, additively manufactured HEAs.

AbstractThe equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy (HEA) possesses excellent properties including exceptional strength–ductility synergy, high corrosion resistance, and good thermal stability. Selective laser melting (SLM) additive manufacturing facilitates the convenient fabrication of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA parts with complex geometries. Here, the SLM process optimization was conducted to achieve a high relative density of as-built CoCrFeNiMn HEA bulks. The mechanisms of process-induced defects and process control were elucidated. The microscale mechanical behaviors were analyzed through in situ scanning electron microscopy observation during the compression tests on micro-pillars of the as-built HEA. The stress–strain characteristics by repeated slip and mechanism of “dislocation avalanche” during the compression of micro-pillars were discussed. The high-cycle fatigue tests of the as-built HEA were performed. It was found that a large number of nano-twins were induced by the fatigue, causing a non-negligible cycle softening phenomenon.
